observation.visible_scene: A clear drinking glass sits on a desk holding two stacked liquid layers—a transparent lower layer and a yellow upper layer—with a green Faber-Castell 9000 pencil leaning inside it, passing through the interface. To the left is a small bottle with a bright yellow cap; behind the glass are a black monitor and keyboard; at the far-left edge a tall clear bottle with a green label is partly in view. Apart from viewpoint motion, the scene is physically static.
visible_changes: The camera/viewpoint drifts slowly over the clip, so the glass, pencil, yellow-capped bottle and background all translate rightward across the frame.
Because of that drift, the tall clear bottle with the green label at the far left becomes progressively more visible (from a thin sliver toward a fuller view).
The pencil keeps the same tilt relative to the glass; its apparent kink/offset at the yellow–clear boundary is a constant refraction artifact, not a real bend or movement.
The two liquid layers stay level and undisturbed—no pouring, stirring or rising bubbles are seen.
A small bluish reflection near the top rim of the glass shifts in step with the camera drift.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the liquids were recently poured or are still settling, and any outcome after the clip, are not shown.
The cause of the apparent motion (handheld shake vs. deliberate pan) is unseen.
uncertain_details: The identities of the liquids (e.g., oil over water) are inferred from appearance only.
It is not fully disambiguated whether the rightward drift is a pure pan or includes slight camera translation.
Minor surface texture changes in the yellow layer are ambiguous—possibly camera shake rather than fluid motion.
